items.prompt: Reviewer A and Reviewer B both correctly spot the same O(n²) bug. Reviewer A's comment stalls the PR for three days; Reviewer B's comment gets a fix in twenty minutes. What actually differed between the two comments?
choices: Reviewer B happened to be explaining a simpler, easier bug, so the three-day gap is really just a difference in bug difficulty
Reviewer A's diagnosis of the quadratic bug was actually wrong, which is why the author pushed back and the fix took three days
The technical fact was identical in both comments — what differed was the social signal about how the author was being treated
Reviewer B is simply a more senior engineer, and senior engineers' comments always get acted on faster regardless of phrasing
items.explanation: Every review comment carries two things at once: a technical fact and a social signal. Both reviewers got the technical fact right. Reviewer A's phrasing signaled judgment of the author; Reviewer B's signaled a shared technical problem — that difference, not the bug itself, is what cost three days.
items.reference:
Technical fact

This will go quadratic

Social signal

Are you being judged or informed?

Why: a comment can be 100% technically correct and still be expensive if the social signal reads as an attack.

items.prompt: Two reviewers file bug reports that are word-for-word identical except for phrasing. One author fixes the code immediately; the other spends time drafting a defense first. What does 'drafting a defense' represent in this unit's model?
choices: Extra work caused by the social signal, not by the technical content of the comment
Proof that the second author disagreed with the bug report
A sign the comment was too short
Something that would happen no matter how the comment was phrased
items.explanation: The defense isn't a response to the bug — it's a response to feeling judged. That's overhead added by the social signal on top of the technical content, and it's exactly the cost this unit's framing techniques are designed to remove.
items.reference:
Technical fact

This will go quadratic

Social signal

Are you being judged or informed?

Why: a comment can be 100% technically correct and still be expensive if the social signal reads as an attack.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between a review comment's technical correctness and its cost to the team?
choices: A technically correct comment always costs the least, since the author just applies the fix with no social overhead no matter how it's phrased
A comment can be technically correct and still be expensive, because the cost includes non-technical overhead like managing a feeling or asking a clarifying question
Cost only comes from comments that are technically wrong, since a correct diagnosis never requires the author to do anything beyond applying the fix
Cost is fixed per bug and doesn't depend on the comment at all, since fixing a given defect takes the same time no matter how it's written
items.explanation: Being right about the bug is necessary but not sufficient for a cheap review exchange. The cost this unit targets is everything the author does that isn't fixing the bug — defending a decision, asking what was meant, or guessing at priority.
items.reference:
Technical fact

This will go quadratic

Social signal

Are you being judged or informed?

Why: a comment can be 100% technically correct and still be expensive if the social signal reads as an attack.

items.prompt: "You did this wrong" and "This will go quadratic once `items` grows" report the same bug. What's the key difference between them?
choices: The first sentence is shorter, and shorter comments are always received better regardless of what they say
The first sentence makes the author the grammatical subject of a judgment; the second makes the code the subject of a prediction
There is no meaningful difference — both sentences report the exact same bug and will land on the author the same way
The second sentence is a lie because it describes a prediction about the future instead of naming what the author actually did
items.explanation: Grammatical subject matters: 'you did this wrong' attaches a judgment directly to a person, while 'this will go quadratic' describes a behavior of the code, predicted from a mechanism. Same defect, different target for the reader to process.
items.reference:
Person-directed: "You did this wrong."
Code-directed: "This will go quadratic once `items` grows."

Why: the grammatical subject decides whether the author feels evaluated or informed, independent of the bug itself.

items.prompt: A reviewer writes: "You forgot the null check." Which rewrite keeps the exact same report but shifts the grammatical subject from the person to the code?
choices: "You really should have caught this before sending it for review."
"This lookup doesn't handle the case where `user` comes back empty."
"Why didn't you handle nulls here? It's a pretty basic case to miss."
"Nice try, but there's a bug in here you'll need to go fix."
items.explanation: "This lookup doesn't handle..." reports the identical gap without naming the author as having failed at anything — the subject is the lookup's behavior, not the person who wrote it.
items.reference:
Person-directed: "You did this wrong."
Code-directed: "This will go quadratic once `items` grows."

Why: the grammatical subject decides whether the author feels evaluated or informed, independent of the bug itself.

items.prompt: Does shifting a comment's subject from the person to the code mean the reviewer should never point out that the author made a specific choice?
choices: Yes, once the subject shifts to the code, the author's specific choices should never be named again
No — it means describing the code's behavior instead of judging the person, not erasing the fact that a person wrote it
Yes, because any comment that shifts the subject to the code is inherently dishonest about who wrote it
No, but the shift only applies to comments about performance, never to comments about correctness
items.explanation: The shift is about where the judgment lands, not about pretending no one wrote the code. "This will go quadratic" still refers to a real choice in the diff — it just doesn't frame that choice as a personal failure.
items.reference:
Person-directed: "You did this wrong."
Code-directed: "This will go quadratic once `items` grows."

Why: the grammatical subject decides whether the author feels evaluated or informed, independent of the bug itself.

items.prompt: "This seems off" and "this lookup on line 42 runs inside the loop, so it'll go quadratic once `items` grows" flag the same concern. What does the vague version force the author to do that the specific version doesn't?
choices: Nothing — both versions require exactly the same amount of diagnostic work from the author either way
Re-read the code and reconstruct the reviewer's diagnosis themselves before they can even evaluate it
Immediately reject the comment as invalid since it doesn't name a specific line or mechanism
Ask the reviewer to just approve the PR anyway without resolving the concern
items.explanation: A vague comment offloads the reviewer's own diagnostic work onto the author, who has to guess what 'off' means before responding at all. A specific comment hands over a diagnosis the author can verify or dispute directly.
items.reference:
Vague: "This seems off."
Specific: "Line 42's lookup runs inside the loop — quadratic once `items` grows."

Why: specificity isn't about length — it's about who does the diagnostic work, reviewer or author.

items.prompt: Is a specific review comment necessarily a longer one?
choices: Yes, specificity always requires spelling things out in more words than a vague comment would
No — specificity is about naming the exact location and mechanism, which can often be done in one short sentence
Yes, because vague comments are structurally always shorter than specific ones in practice
No, specificity has nothing to do with naming a location or mechanism at all
items.explanation: Specificity is about content (what line, what mechanism, what condition), not word count. A one-sentence comment that names the exact line and the exact failure mode is more specific than a long comment that never says where or why.
items.reference:
Vague: "This seems off."
Specific: "Line 42's lookup runs inside the loop — quadratic once `items` grows."

Why: specificity isn't about length — it's about who does the diagnostic work, reviewer or author.

items.prompt: In a live conversation, a pause after a comment usually means the other person is thinking. What does an equivalent silence typically mean in an async PR review thread?
choices: The exact same thing — silence always means the reviewer is still thinking it over, just like a live pause
Nothing — silence never carries any information at all in an async review thread
It's ambiguous: it could mean the reviewer is still looking, is done, or is waiting on the author, with no way to tell which
It always means the reviewer disagrees with the change and is drafting a longer objection
items.explanation: Live conversation supplies tone and immediacy that make a pause interpretable. Async review strips that out, so silence is ambiguous by default — which is exactly why stated response-time norms matter in async review.
items.reference:
Live: a pause = thinking.
Async: silence = ambiguous — reviewing? busy? waiting on you?

Why: async strips out the cues that make silence interpretable, so norms have to replace them.

items.prompt: Why does async PR review benefit from an explicit, team-wide response-time norm (e.g. 'first pass within one business day')?
choices: Because it guarantees every bug reported in the PR gets fixed correctly on the first attempt, with no further back-and-forth needed
Because without it, both the author and reviewer default to worst-case assumptions about silence, since async has no equivalent of a live conversational pause
Because most version control tools require a stated response-time norm before a PR can be merged into the main branch
Because it removes the need for the reviewer to leave any comments on the diff at all, replacing review entirely
items.explanation: A stated norm replaces an assumption both sides would otherwise have to guess at. Without it, silence is read pessimistically by default, adding social friction that has nothing to do with the actual code.
items.reference:
Live: a pause = thinking.
Async: silence = ambiguous — reviewing? busy? waiting on you?

Why: async strips out the cues that make silence interpretable, so norms have to replace them.

items.prompt: Which of these is a genuinely async-specific concern for PR review, as opposed to something that would matter equally in a live conversation?
choices: Whether the reviewer used correct grammar and spelling in their comment
Whether the code actually contains the bug the reviewer thinks it does
Whether the author can tell if silence after a comment means 'still reviewing' or 'waiting on you'
Whether the PR description has a clear, descriptive title summarizing the change
items.explanation: A live conversation makes this ambiguity disappear automatically — you can just ask, or read the pause. Async review has no such built-in signal, which is why interpreting silence is a problem specific to the async medium.
items.reference:
Live: a pause = thinking.
Async: silence = ambiguous — reviewing? busy? waiting on you?

Why: async strips out the cues that make silence interpretable, so norms have to replace them.

items.prompt: A reviewer leaves ten unlabeled comments — one is a genuine data-loss bug, nine are style nits. What's the most likely author behavior, and why?
choices: The author ignores all ten comments equally, treating the bug and the nits as the same priority
The author fixes the data-loss bug first automatically, since severity is always obvious from the bug itself
The author can't tell which comment is blocking, so they may spend disproportionate time on the nits or treat everything with equal priority
The author asks the reviewer to resubmit the whole PR as ten separate smaller pull requests
items.explanation: Without a severity signal, the author has no way to distinguish a must-fix from a nice-to-have, so priority has to be guessed — and guessing under time pressure doesn't reliably favor the comment that matters most.
items.reference:
10 comments, unlabeled: 1 blocking bug + 9 nits, indistinguishable at a glance.

Why: technical correctness of each comment doesn't establish priority across a batch — that has to be stated separately.

items.prompt: According to this unit's cost model, which of these is the actual 'expensive' part of a poorly-framed review comment?
choices: The time it takes the reviewer to type out the comment in the first place
The bug itself, regardless of how it's reported, since a defect costs the same to fix no matter what
Whatever the author has to do that isn't fixing the bug — managing a feeling, asking a clarifying question, or guessing at priority
The number of characters in the comment, since longer comments always take longer to read and act on
items.explanation: The pattern across every costly example in this unit is the same: the expense isn't the defect, it's the extra non-technical work — defending, clarifying, or guessing — that bad framing adds on top of it.
items.reference:
10 comments, unlabeled: 1 blocking bug + 9 nits, indistinguishable at a glance.

Why: technical correctness of each comment doesn't establish priority across a batch — that has to be stated separately.

items.prompt: This unit's model names three levers that turn a costly comment into a cheap one. What are they?
choices: Length, formatting, and emoji use, since how polished a comment looks determines how it's received
Subject (person vs. code), specificity, and framing as a question vs. a statement
Seniority of the reviewer, time of day the comment was left, and overall size of the PR
Programming language used, size of the team, and whether CI is currently passing
items.explanation: The three levers are: who the grammatical subject is (person or code), how specific the ask is (vague or named-and-located), and whether the suggestion is framed as an instruction or a question.
items.reference:
LeverCostlyLower-cost
SubjectYou did this wrongThis will go quadratic
SpecificityThis seems offLine 42, quadratic once items grows
FramingUse a hashmapWorth swapping to a Map here?

items.prompt: A reviewer applies only the 'subject' lever (person → code) but leaves a comment vague and phrased as a command. Has the reviewer applied the full model?
choices: Yes, applying any single lever from the model is equivalent to applying all three levers at once, since they overlap in effect
No — the three levers are independent; fixing subject alone doesn't add the missing location/mechanism or soften the instruction into a question
No, because specificity is actually the only lever of the three that has any real effect on how a comment lands
Yes, because subject is the one lever that fully determines whether a comment lands well, making the other two redundant
items.explanation: Each lever fixes a different gap: subject affects whether the author feels judged, specificity affects whether they can act without guessing, and framing affects whether they can respond rather than just comply. Applying one doesn't substitute for the others.
items.reference:
LeverCostlyLower-cost
SubjectYou did this wrongThis will go quadratic
SpecificityThis seems offLine 42, quadratic once items grows
FramingUse a hashmapWorth swapping to a Map here?

items.prompt: "The inner loop over `discount_codes` re-scans the full list for every order — worth building a lookup dict first?" Which levers does this comment apply?
choices: None — despite naming a specific line, it's still phrased as a vague instruction with no real mechanism given
Only the framing lever — the subject is still the author and the mechanism still isn't named
All three: code-directed subject, specific mechanism, and framed as a question
Only specificity — the sentence still reads as a command rather than a question
items.explanation: The subject is the loop (not the author), it names the exact mechanism (re-scanning for every order), and it ends with a question rather than a command — all three levers are present at once.
items.reference:
LeverCostlyLower-cost
SubjectYou did this wrongThis will go quadratic
SpecificityThis seems offLine 42, quadratic once items grows
FramingUse a hashmapWorth swapping to a Map here?

items.prompt: "Use a hashmap" and "Worth swapping to a Map here?" suggest the identical fix. Why might the question form get a better response even when the reviewer's suggestion is correct?
choices: Because questions are always processed faster by a reader than an equivalent plain declarative sentence would be
Because a flat instruction positions the author as an executor of someone else's decision, while a question leaves room for context the reviewer doesn't have yet
Because the author can simply ignore a question without that counting as declining a reviewer's direct request to change something
There's no real difference — a reader responds to a question and an instruction in exactly the same way either way
items.explanation: A command assumes the reviewer's solution is the only one worth considering. A question invites a response — either agreement, or context the reviewer was missing — without forcing the author to argue against a directive just to raise it.
items.reference:
Instruction: "Use a hashmap."
Question: "Worth swapping to a Map here?"

Why: a question survives being wrong; an instruction has to be defied to be corrected.

items.prompt: Suppose the reviewer's suggestion is actually wrong because of context they don't have. Which framing resolves that mismatch in fewer round-trips?
choices: A flat instruction, because it forces the author to respond with the missing context right away
A question, because it gives the author room to explain the missing context without first having to disagree with a directive
Neither — the framing of the comment has no measurable effect on how many round-trips a thread takes
A flat instruction, because questions in review threads are usually left unanswered
items.explanation: With a question, the author can just answer with the missing context in one reply. With an instruction, the author often has to push back against the directive itself before the missing context even gets raised — an extra social step, and sometimes an extra round-trip.
items.reference:
Instruction: "Use a hashmap."
Question: "Worth swapping to a Map here?"

Why: a question survives being wrong; an instruction has to be defied to be corrected.

items.prompt: Does framing a suggestion as a question mean the reviewer can no longer state a clear preferred fix?
choices: Yes, a question can never name a specific solution without the sentence turning into an instruction in disguise
No — a question can still name the exact fix ('Worth swapping to a Map here?') while leaving room for the author to respond rather than comply
Yes, because naming a specific fix inside a sentence always reads as a command no matter how the sentence actually ends
No, but only when the reviewer happens to outrank the author somewhere on the team's org chart
items.explanation: A question isn't vague by necessity — it can be exactly as specific as a statement. The only thing that changes is the grammatical form at the end: does the sentence assume compliance, or invite a response.
items.reference:
Instruction: "Use a hashmap."
Question: "Worth swapping to a Map here?"

Why: a question survives being wrong; an instruction has to be defied to be corrected.

items.prompt: A reviewer sends five separate one-line comments over two hours instead of one batched review with all five points, on a PR the author is actively trying to finish. What's the likely downside of the drip-feed approach?
choices: There is no downside — five separate comments always give strictly better coverage than one combined review
The author gets interrupted repeatedly and can't tell if the review is complete or more comments are still coming
Drip-fed comments are always technically wrong because they weren't thought through as a single pass
It guarantees the PR merges faster than it would with one batched round of review
items.explanation: Batching related comments into one review pass lets the author address everything in one sitting and know when review is actually done. A drip-feed creates repeated interruptions and uncertainty about whether more feedback is still coming.
items.reference:
Drip-fed: 5 comments over 2 hrs, author unsure if done.
Batched: 1 pass, author knows the full scope at once.

Why: batching turns review into one predictable interruption instead of several unpredictable ones.

items.prompt: Why does batching related review comments together (submitted as one review) generally cost the author less than the same comments arriving one at a time?
choices: Because comments submitted together as part of one batch are always phrased more concisely than standalone ones would be
Because the author can address the full set in one sitting instead of being interrupted repeatedly with uncertainty about whether more are coming
Because submitting a batched review automatically rewrites and corrects any vague comments contained within it
There's no cost difference — a drip-feed and a single batch land on the author's workflow in exactly the same way
items.explanation: The cost isn't about comment quality here — it's about interruption pattern. One predictable batch lets the author plan a single focused pass; a drip-feed forces context-switching every time a new comment lands.
items.reference:
Drip-fed: 5 comments over 2 hrs, author unsure if done.
Batched: 1 pass, author knows the full scope at once.

Why: batching turns review into one predictable interruption instead of several unpredictable ones.

items.prompt: What problem does labeling comments `nit:` (optional) or `blocking:` (must-fix) solve that the three individual-comment levers (subject, specificity, framing) don't address on their own?
choices: It fixes grammar and spelling issues across all the comments in a batch at once
It communicates priority across a whole batch of comments, which no single comment's wording can convey on its own
It makes every comment in the batch automatically technically correct
It replaces the need for the reviewer to ever be specific about location or mechanism
items.explanation: The three levers govern how one comment lands. Severity labels are a batch-level signal: they tell the author which comment to act on first, something that isn't knowable from reading any single comment in isolation.
items.reference:
nit: optional polish — blocking: must-fix before merge.

Why: unlabeled batches force the author to guess priority, and guessing under pressure isn't reliable.

items.prompt: A reviewer leaves eight unlabeled comments; one is a data-loss bug, the rest are style nits. What does this unit predict happens?
choices: The author automatically prioritizes the data-loss bug first, since severity is always self-evident just from reading a comment
The author may spend disproportionate time on the nits, or treat every comment as equal priority, because nothing signals which one actually blocks the merge
The reviewer's eight comments are ignored entirely by the author because there are simply too many of them to act on at once
The PR merges automatically regardless of what any of the eight unlabeled comments actually say about the code
items.explanation: Technical correctness of a comment doesn't establish priority relative to the rest of the batch — that has to be communicated explicitly, through labels or sequencing, or the author is left guessing under time pressure.
items.reference:
nit: optional polish — blocking: must-fix before merge.

Why: unlabeled batches force the author to guess priority, and guessing under pressure isn't reliable.

items.prompt: Does marking a comment `nit:` mean the underlying suggestion is unimportant or shouldn't be raised at all?
choices: Yes, a `nit:` label means the observation shouldn't have been left in the review thread at all in the first place
No — `nit:` still raises a real observation, it just signals the author can decide whether to act on it before merging, unlike a `blocking:` item
Yes, `nit:` is really just a polite, indirect way for a reviewer to criticize the author without saying so outright
No, `nit:` and `blocking:` carry exactly the same weight and urgency for the author reading the thread
items.explanation: `nit:` doesn't mean the observation is worthless — it means the author has discretion. The label communicates priority, not validity; a nit can still be a good suggestion the author simply isn't required to act on before merging.
items.reference:
nit: optional polish — blocking: must-fix before merge.

Why: unlabeled batches force the author to guess priority, and guessing under pressure isn't reliable.

items.prompt: In the sequence diagram from L2, why does the author end up 'fixing everything to be safe' after a two-day silent gap followed by eight unlabeled comments?
choices: Because all eight comments left in that batch happened to be genuinely equally severe, so treating them identically was actually the correct call here

Because the combination of no response-time norm and no severity labels leaves the author with no reliable signal for what actually matters, so treating everything as equally urgent is the safest guess
Because the author in this particular example happens to enjoy polishing style nitpicks more than fixing substantive logic bugs in the diff
Because the reviewer explicitly asked, somewhere earlier in the thread, for every single one of the eight comments to be addressed before merge
items.explanation: Two missing signals stack here: no response-time norm made the silence ambiguous, and no severity labels made the batch's priority unreadable. With both missing, treating every comment as equally urgent is the author's only safe default.
items.reference:
No response norm + no severity labels = author defaults to fixing everything, just in case.

Why: two missing signals compound — each alone is recoverable, together they force the costliest guess.

items.prompt: What do severity labels and a stated response-time norm have in common, in terms of what they actually do?
choices: Both deliberately slow down the review process so the author has more time to respond
Both replace something the author would otherwise have to guess at with information the reviewer already has and can simply state
Both are purely cosmetic conventions that have no measurable effect on how the author behaves
Both are features required by most version control systems before a PR can be merged
items.explanation: Both are the same underlying move as the three individual-comment levers: converting private information the reviewer already has (this one's optional, I'll look again tomorrow) into something explicit, instead of leaving the author to infer it.
items.reference:
No response norm + no severity labels = author defaults to fixing everything, just in case.

Why: two missing signals compound — each alone is recoverable, together they force the costliest guess.

items.prompt: In the `apply_discounts` rewrite, the step 'This inner loop is wrong — use a hashmap' applies which single lever from L2, and what's still missing after that step?
choices: Applies specificity; the framing and subject levers are both still missing from the comment
Applies the subject lever (code, not person); location, mechanism, and question framing are still missing
Applies all three levers at once — subject, specificity, and question framing
Applies framing as a question; the subject and specificity levers are both still missing
items.explanation: Moving from 'you' to 'this inner loop' only fixes the subject. The comment still doesn't say which line or why it's slow (specificity), and it's still phrased as a command (framing) — those come in the next two steps.
items.reference:
StepComment
Original"This is wrong, use a hashmap."
+ Subject"This inner loop is wrong — use a hashmap."
+ Specificity"...line 6 re-scans the full list — O(orders × codes)."
+ Framing"...worth building a dict once before the loop?"

items.prompt: The fully rewritten comment about `apply_discounts` is longer, in characters, than the original 'This is wrong, use a hashmap.' What does the unit say about that length increase?
choices: It proves the rewritten version is actually worse overall, since a longer comment always takes noticeably more time for the author to read through
The extra length is cheaper for the author overall, because it removes the need for the author to reconstruct the location and mechanism themselves
Length is entirely irrelevant to cost in either direction — a comment's raw character count has no bearing on how it lands with the reader
It means the reviewer was padding the comment with unnecessary detail that the author genuinely didn't need in order to act on it
items.explanation: The original was never cheap because it was short — it was expensive because it was missing information the author then had to reconstruct. A longer comment that supplies that information directly costs the reviewer more to write but costs the author, and the exchange as a whole, less.
items.reference:
StepComment
Original"This is wrong, use a hashmap."
+ Subject"This inner loop is wrong — use a hashmap."
+ Specificity"...line 6 re-scans the full list — O(orders × codes)."
+ Framing"...worth building a dict once before the loop?"

items.prompt: Suppose the author of `apply_discounts` has a real reason not to cache the lookup (say, `discount_codes` gets mutated mid-loop elsewhere). What does the fully-rewritten, question-framed comment let the author do that a flat 'use a hashmap' instruction wouldn't?
choices: Nothing different — a flat instruction and a question both force the exact same response out of the author either way
Answer directly with the missing context in one reply, resolving the thread in a single round-trip instead of pushing back against a directive first
Ignore the comment entirely, since a question-framed comment never actually needs a reply the way an instruction does
Escalate immediately to a synchronous call regardless of how the original comment happened to be framed
items.explanation: A question gives the author a legitimate opening to supply missing context in one reply. A flat instruction tends to require the author to first disagree with the directive before the missing context even gets raised, costing an extra round-trip.
items.reference:
StepComment
Original"This is wrong, use a hashmap."
+ Subject"This inner loop is wrong — use a hashmap."
+ Specificity"...line 6 re-scans the full list — O(orders × codes)."
+ Framing"...worth building a dict once before the loop?"

items.prompt: Why does naming an exact line number and mechanism ("line 6 re-scans the full list for every order") matter more in an async PR comment than it would in a live pairing session?
choices: It doesn't matter more — a line number carries exactly the same weight in a live pairing session as it does async
In a live session the reviewer can just point at the screen; async has no equivalent, so the comment itself has to carry that location information
It doesn't, because most modern async review tools don't actually support leaving a comment on a specific line
Line numbers only start to matter once a file has grown past a few hundred lines of code total
items.explanation: Live pairing lets a reviewer point, gesture, or say 'this part' while looking at the same screen. Async comments lose that entirely — if the comment doesn't name the exact location and mechanism, the author has to hunt for what's being referred to.
items.reference:
Live: reviewer can point at the screen.
Async: the comment itself must carry the location.

Why: async strips out pointing and gesture, so precision has to move into the text.

items.prompt: A comment says 'this function has a bug' with no line reference, on a 40-line diff. What does the author have to do before they can even start evaluating the claim?
choices: Nothing — the claim is immediately actionable
Search the whole diff themselves to guess which part the reviewer means
Automatically assume it's the last line changed
Reject the comment as invalid
items.explanation: Without a location, the author has to do the reviewer's pointing for them — scanning the diff and guessing which part is meant, which is exactly the diagnostic work a specific, line-referenced comment would have skipped.
items.reference:
Live: reviewer can point at the screen.
Async: the comment itself must carry the location.

Why: async strips out pointing and gesture, so precision has to move into the text.

items.prompt: The `load_user_preferences` function interpolates `user_id` directly into a SQL string — a SQL injection bug. Why is 'Worth using a parameterized query here, in case user_id isn't always trustworthy?' a mistake for this specific comment, even though it correctly applies the question-framing lever?
choices: Because a question is always the wrong framing choice to reach for, no matter what category or severity of bug is actually being reported
Because it frames a must-fix security defect as an optional consideration a reader might reasonably decline, when it should be marked blocking and stated as fact
Because parameterized queries aren't actually a valid, working fix for a SQL injection vulnerability shaped like this one
Because the sentence itself is grammatically awkward in a way that makes it genuinely hard for the author to parse quickly
items.explanation: The three levers reduce unnecessary friction — they aren't a rule to soften every comment regardless of stakes. A skimmed batch reads 'worth considering' as low-priority, which is exactly the wrong signal for a defect that must be fixed before merge.
items.reference:
SituationRight framing
Optional/non-urgentQuestion, nit: if optional
Design disagreementQuestion, invites reasoning
Security/data-loss bugStatement, blocking:, no softening

items.prompt: What does the corrected SQL-injection comment keep from the three-lever technique, and what does it deliberately drop?
choices: It keeps nothing from the technique at all and reverts fully to the original blunt, person-directed style
It keeps code-directed subject and specificity, but drops the soft question framing in favor of a direct statement with a blocking: label
It keeps the soft question framing from before, but drops the specific line reference and mechanism
It drops the code-directed subject entirely and names the author as having caused the vulnerability
items.explanation: The corrected version is still code-directed and names the exact mechanism and fix — it just states the defect as fact with an explicit severity marker instead of offering it as an optional question, because this is not a matter of opinion.
items.reference:
SituationRight framing
Optional/non-urgentQuestion, nit: if optional
Design disagreementQuestion, invites reasoning
Security/data-loss bugStatement, blocking:, no softening

items.prompt: According to the situation table in L3, what framing fits a genuine design disagreement where reasonable people could differ (e.g. one function vs. two)?
choices: A blocking: statement with no room for discussion, same as a security bug
A question that invites the author's reasoning, since the 'right' answer isn't settled
Silence — design disagreements should never be raised in review
A nit:, since design disagreements never matter
items.explanation: Unlike a security defect, a design disagreement doesn't have one objectively correct answer, so framing it as settled fact would overclaim. A question invites the author's reasoning, which is the appropriate move when the matter is genuinely debatable.
items.reference:
SituationRight framing
Optional/non-urgentQuestion, nit: if optional

items.prompt: According to L3's escalation flowchart, what specific signal indicates a comment thread should move to a sync call instead of another async reply?
choices: The author pushed back and disagreed with the reviewer's suggestion even once in the thread
Two full round-trips have passed with no new information on either side — positions are being restated, not refined
The thread has grown to more than three total comments between the author and reviewer
The reviewer leaving the comment happens to be more senior than the author of the PR
items.explanation: One round of disagreement is normal and often resolves with more detail. The escalation signal is specifically two rounds with no new information — a sign the async medium itself, not the wording, is the bottleneck.
items.reference:
Signal to escalate: 2 round-trips, zero new information either time.

Why: a better comment fixes round-trip 1's cost — it can't manufacture information that doesn't exist in text yet.

items.prompt: A reviewer and author have gone two rounds on a design disagreement with no new information either time. The reviewer's instinct is to write a third, even more carefully worded comment. Is this the right move?
choices: Yes, a more carefully worded third comment will generally resolve a disagreement that two comments couldn't
No — the stuck signal has already been met, so a well-framed comment can't fix it because the bottleneck is the medium, not the wording
Yes, because adding another comment to the thread always introduces new information to consider
No, the thread should simply be abandoned and the PR closed without any resolution
items.explanation: A third comment assumes the first two weren't clear enough, but the actual diagnosis is that both sides already understand each other's position and still disagree — that's a medium problem a live conversation solves in minutes, not a wording problem another comment can fix.
items.reference:
Signal to escalate: 2 round-trips, zero new information either time.

Why: a better comment fixes round-trip 1's cost — it can't manufacture information that doesn't exist in text yet.

items.prompt: Why is a terse, well-intentioned async reply like 'no' or 'fix it' especially risky compared to the same brevity in a live conversation?
choices: Terse replies carry exactly the same risk in both a live conversation and an async text thread
Text strips out tone of voice, so a short reply that would sound neutral spoken aloud can read as curt or dismissive in writing
Terse async replies are risky only because they're statistically more likely to be technically incorrect
This risk only applies if the person reading the reply isn't a fluent speaker of the language it's written in
items.explanation: The async medium removes tone-of-voice cues that would normally soften a short spoken reply. The same words, stripped of vocal tone, can land as curt or dismissive in text even when no dismissiveness was intended.
items.reference:
Spoken "no": tone softens it. Written "no": tone is gone, reads flat or curt.

Why: text has no vocal channel, so brevity that's fine live can misfire in writing.

items.prompt: Does the risk of terse async replies mean every review comment should be long and heavily qualified?
choices: Yes, every single review comment sent through an async thread should be long and heavily qualified so it can't possibly be misread
No — a specific, code-directed, question-framed comment can still be short; the risk is specifically with bare, context-free terseness, not length itself
Yes, because a short comment is structurally incapable of being both technically correct and fully complete at the same time
No, the length of a written comment has no relationship at all to how the person reading it is likely to perceive its tone
items.explanation: The three levers from L2 show that a short comment can still carry subject, specificity, and framing correctly (e.g. 'Worth swapping to a Map here?'). The risk is bare terseness with no context, not brevity in general.
items.reference:
Spoken "no": tone softens it. Written "no": tone is gone, reads flat or curt.

Why: text has no vocal channel, so brevity that's fine live can misfire in writing.

items.prompt: If a PR gets three independent reviewers commenting on overlapping parts of the same diff, each unaware of the others, what new problem appears that doesn't exist with a single reviewer?
choices: No new problem appears at all — three independent reviewers are strictly equivalent to one reviewer leaving the exact same comments three times
The author may have to reconcile conflicting or overlapping feedback across three separate threads, on top of judging each comment's severity and framing individually
Three independent reviewers will always agree with each other automatically about every single point they each happen to raise
The PR can no longer be merged under any circumstances once a third independent reviewer has left even one comment
items.explanation: With multiple independent reviewers, the author's workload isn't just 'apply the levers to each comment' — it now includes reconciling potentially conflicting feedback across threads, a batch-level problem that scales with reviewer count, not just comment count.
items.reference:
1 reviewer: author judges each comment.
3 reviewers: author also reconciles overlap/conflict across threads.

Why: etiquette that works for one reviewer doesn't automatically scale to many without added coordination.

items.prompt: With three reviewers commenting independently, does the 'two round-trips, no new information' escalation signal from a two-person thread still mean exactly the same thing?
choices: Yes, the escalation signal stays completely unaffected no matter how many independent reviewers happen to be commenting on the same diff at once

Not exactly — the author may now be fielding multiple threads at once, so a team may need additional etiquette (e.g. reviewers coordinating before commenting, or a lead reviewer resolving conflicts) beyond what a single-reviewer signal covers
No, because once a third reviewer gets involved, no single comment thread between any two people can ever actually be considered stuck
Yes, because the total number of reviewers active on a given PR has no bearing whatsoever on how async review etiquette should work
items.explanation: The signal still applies within any one thread, but three simultaneous threads add a coordination problem the original two-person model didn't need to solve — which is exactly the kind of scaling question worth extending the unit's model to answer.
items.reference:
1 reviewer: author judges each comment.
3 reviewers: author also reconciles overlap/conflict across threads.

Why: etiquette that works for one reviewer doesn't automatically scale to many without added coordination.
